content: Nafcillin is an antibiotic commonly used to treat infections caused by specific types of bacteria. However, it is not effective against all infections, as some bacteria may have developed resistance to it. It is also ineffective against viral infections such as the common cold, influenza, or coronavirus, as well as other non-bacterial infections. Using nafcillin or any antibiotic unnecessarily can lead to reduced effectiveness in treating bacterial infections in the future. Your healthcare provider may also prescribe nafcillin for other conditions as deemed appropriate. Nafcillin works by inhibiting the ability of certain bacteria to form their cell walls, which is essential for their survival. Nafcillin is available in injectable forms, including 1 g, 2 g, 10 g, and 20 mg/mL injections, as well as 2 g/100 mL injections. It is typically administered by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinical setting. If you miss a dose of nafcillin, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and proceed with your regular dosing schedule. Do not take double or extra doses. It is crucial to complete the full prescribed course of nafcillin, even if your symptoms improve, to prevent the development of antibiotic resistance. In the event of an overdose, seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. Overdosing on nafcillin may require discontinuation of the medication, and your healthcare provider will manage your symptoms and provide supportive care as needed. Common side effects of nafcillin include pain, swelling, or inflammation at the injection site, as well as rash. If these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here, so contact your provider if you suspect any adverse reactions. Serious side effects of nafcillin, though less common, include severe allergic reactions, seizures, kidney damage, liver damage, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, and blood disorders. Symptoms of severe allergic reactions include breathing difficulties, wheezing, rapid heartbeat, fever, swollen lymph nodes, facial or throat swelling, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or fainting. If you experience any of these, stop using nafcillin and seek emergency medical care. Seizures have been reported in some individuals using nafcillin. Signs of a seizure include muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, stiffening of the arms and legs, confusion, dizziness, or loss of consciousness. If you notice these symptoms, discontinue nafcillin and contact your healthcare provider immediately. Kidney damage may occur with nafcillin use. Symptoms include reduced urination, swelling in the feet or legs, unusual fatigue, chest pain, confusion, or nausea. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience these symptoms. Liver damage, also known as hepatotoxicity, is another potential risk. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, fatigue, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stools, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you notice these signs. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), can occur during or up to two months after stopping nafcillin. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe abdominal cramps, or fever. Seek medical attention if these symptoms arise. Nafcillin can also cause blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, neutropenia, or bone marrow depression. Symptoms include fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual fatigue, dizziness, or abnormal heart rhythms. Stop using nafcillin and seek immediate medical care if you experience these symptoms. Nafcillin should not be used by individuals allergic to nafcillin or any of its ingredients. Your pharmacist can provide a complete list of ingredients in the specific product dispensed. Inform your healthcare provider of any allergies, including those to penicillin, other medications, or corn products. Before using nafcillin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions, including asthma, liver or kidney disease, a history of antibiotic-associated diarrhea, or if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Nafcillin passes into breast milk, so discuss the risks and benefits with your provider. Nafcillin may interact with other medications, including tetracyclines, warfarin, cyclosporine, and probenecid. Always inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and over-the-counter medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are taking to avoid potential interactions. There are no known interactions between nafcillin and food or drinks. However, heavy alcohol consumption may impair your immune response and hinder your body’s ability to fight infections. Discuss alcohol use with your healthcare provider. If you have any concerns or questions about nafcillin, consult your healthcare provider for guidance.
